title: Lecture 2 – Refraction
html:
Source: c2 refraction.pptx – 64 slides

REFRACTION #1

REFRACTION #2

  • splits white light into it component spectral colors.
  • Red is refracted least,
  • blue is refracted most.

Ocular refraction #3

  • defined as
  • the ratio of the refractive power of the lens and cornea(the refractive media) to the axial length of the globe
  • the eye is a dioptric optical system (60-65D)
  • due to clear optical media
  • the cornea, 45 D
  • aqueous humor,
  • vitreous,
  • lens. 15-20 D

D= 1/f. #4

  • The refractive power D (in diopters) of an optical system is the reciprocal of the focal length of a lens f (in meters).

Slide 5 #5

  • The converging lens (biconvex) concentrates incident light rays at a focal point behind the lens.
  • Where a lens focuses parallel incident light rays 0.5m behind the lens, the refractive power is 1/0.5m= + 2D.

The diverging lens (biconcave) ensures that the light rays do not meet at all. #6

  • The light rays appear to originate at a virtual focal point in front of the lens.
  • Where the virtual focal point is in front of the lens, the refractive power is 1/–0.5m = –2 D.

Ocular refraction #7

  • Methods of examination
  • Subiective
  • Donders’ technique.
  • successively placing various combinations of lenses before the patient’s eye until the maximum visual acuity is reached
  • Obiective
  • skiascopy, astigmometry,
  • ophthalmoscopy,
  • refractometry

Ocular refraction #8

  • Methods of examination
  • Obiective
  • skiascopy, astigmometry,
  • ophthalmoscopy,
  • refractometry

Ocular refraction #9

  • Methods of examination
  • skiascopy, retinoscopy
  • The retina is illuminated through the pupil.
  • The examiner observes the optical phenomena in the patient’s pupil while moving the light source

Ocular refraction #10

  • Methods of examination
  • Refractometry
  • ophthalmoscopic observation of a test image projected on to the patient’s retina.
  • The distance between the test and the eye is changed until the image appears in focus on the retina.
  • Refraction can be calculated from the measured values.
  • An alternative to changing of the distance is to place various lenses in the path of the light beam.
  • Automated refractometry.
  • measures automatically with light-sensitive detectors and a computer until a focused image appears on the retina.
  • operate with infrared light.

1. Statical refraction #11

  • considered when the eye looks at the infinite,
  • a status in which the light rays entering the eye are parallel.
  • Ophthalmological infinite
  • a distance of >5 metres off the eye
  • the rays enter parallel the eye.

1. Statical refraction #12

  • Emmetropia
  • normal statical refraction
  • The ratio of the axial length of the eye to the refractive power of the cornea and lens is balanced.
  • not necessarily identical to good visual acuity.
  • other disorders that reduce visual acuity, (atrophy of the optic nerve,amblyopia).

1. Statical refraction #13

  • Emmetropia
  • Parallel light rays that enter the eye meet at a focal point on the retina
  • not anterior or posterior , (ametropia)

1. Statical refraction #14

  • Refractive errors
  • Ametropia
  • a mismatch between the axial length of the eye and the refractive power of the lens and cornea.
  • axial, common,
  • refractive, less frequently
  • disturbances of the statical refraction
  • hypermetropia,
  • myopia,
  • astigmatism

1. Statical refraction #15

  • A)Hypermetropia (hyperopia)
  • discrepancy between the refractive power and axial length of the eye
  • parallel incident light rays converge at a focal point posterior to the retina

1. Statical refraction #16

  • A)Hypermetropia
  • the most widespread disturbance of statical refraction
  • usually early in the first years of the life
  • the eye is not completely developed
  • declines progressively through childhood
  • as the child grows up the eye becomes emmetropic or even myopic in the teenage years

1. Statical refraction #17

  • A)Hypemetropia
  • the image of an object form behind the retina
  • only by accommodation can be brought on the retina

1. Statical refraction #18

  • A)Hypemetropia
  • Symptoms:
  • In young patients, accommodation can compensate for slight to moderate hyperopia. this leads to chronic overuse of the ciliary muscle.
  • Reading can cause asthenopic symptoms eye
  • pain or headache,
  • burning sensation in the eyes,
  • blepharoconjunctivitis,
  • blurred vision, rapid fatigue.
  • hyperopic persons tend to become presbyopic early.
  • convergent strabismus with amblyopia
  • excessive over accommodation
  • disturbing the normal relation between convergence and accommodation
  • a break in the balance of the position of the ocular globes

Classification of hypermetropia #19

  • etiology:
  • Axial
  • the anteroposterior axis is too short;
  • Index
  • refraction of the ocular media is lower than normal;
  • Curvature
  • the corneal curvature is reduced
  • Decreased refractive power

Classification of hypermetropia #20

  • b) size degree hypermetropias :
  • small (<3 diopters)
  • medium (>3 and <6 diopters);
  • larger (>6 diopters)
  • when >10 diopters, aphakia must be suspected.

Diagnostic considerations #21

  • The full extent of hyperopia includes
  • latent hyperopia
  • clinically manifest hyperopia.
  • latent hyperopia
  • The ciliary muscle is chronically under tension to compensate
  • This leads to a residual accommodation in which the muscle is unable to relax even after the hyperopia has been corrected with plus lenses.
  • paralyzing the ciliary body with cycloplegic agents cyclopentolate or atropine.

Diagnostic considerations #22

  • In the presence of asthenopic symptoms of uncertain origin, refraction testing under cycloplegia is indicated to rule out latent hyperopia.

Management #23

  • Optical,
  • spherical convergent glasses.
  • the strongest convergent glasses that the patient is able to achieve maximum VA.
  • Addition for near vision to substitute the missing accommodation.
  • In children a total correction is needed to prevent strabismus.
  • soft contact lenses.
  • Correction of aphakia

Management #24

  • Surgical,
  • excimer laser
  • may correct an up to 6 D hypermetropia.
  • Correction of aphakia

B)Myopia #25

  • A discrepancy between the refractive power and axial length of the eye
  • parallel incident light rays converge at a focal point anterior to the retina
  • The myopic eye can only produce sharply defined images of close objects from which the light rays diverge until they enter the eye

B)Myopia #26

  • less frequently than hypermetropia
  • Hyper development of the globe.
  • the eye is longer than average

Classification  of myopia #27

  • etiology:
  • axial
  • the anteroposterior axis of the globe longer than normal;
  • index
  • the refractive index of the ocular media greater than normal
  • curvature
  • the corneal curvature is increased.

Classification  of myopia #28

  • size degree
  • simple (<6-7 D)
  • congenital (20D and 40D).

Simple myopia (school myopia) #29

  • it appears at 6-7 years of age not exceeding 6-7 diopters
  • may slowly evolve until 20-25 years of age when it comes to a standstill
  • Etiology.
  • heredity and unfavorable conditions of visual work;
  • Classification.
  • small (<3 diopters),
  • medium (3 by 6 diopters)
  • large (>6 diopters).
  • Particularities.
  • The patient does not see well at the distance
  • sees very well in the nearness.

Simple myopia #30

  • Management
  • a) Optical
  • concave glasses,
  • the weakest glasses to achieve maximum VA
  • In small myopia same glasses for distance and nearness.
  • Medium and large myopias two pairs of glasses
  • stronger for distance and another weaker
  • for near vision (60% from the distance glasses)
  • soft contact lenses.

Simple myopia #31

  • Management
  • b) Surgical
  • excimer laser
  • Refractive surgery
  • anterior chamber intraocular lens (diverging lens)
  • Lens removal (rare)

Congenital myopia #32

  • malignant, degenerative and pathological
  • large eyes very decreased sight
  • floaters within the vitreous
  • Opacities “flying flies” (vitreous degeneration)
  • degenerative chorioretinal lesions at fundus,(choroidosis)
  • near the papilla
  • large myopic crescent
  • within the macula
  • hemorrhages and the following fibrosis -“Fuchs spot”
  • Cataract (subcapsular posterior lens opacities )
  • retinal detachment
  • the most dangerous complication

Management #33

  • Optical
  • spherical concave glasses (subtotal correction)
  • soft contact lenses
  • allow a very close correction to the dioptrical value of myopia
  • Medical
  • improvement of chorioretinal nourishment
  • vasodilating drugs vitamins A and E, systemically

Management #34

  • Surgical
  • refractive surgery (excimer laser)
  • lens refractive surgery
  • phakic artificial lens with negative power
  • extraction of clear lens followed by artificial lens implantation)
  • surgical treatment of complications (cataract RD)

C) Astigmatism #35

  • aspherical refractive disturbance.
  • from the Greek word stigma (point)
  • lack of a focal point.
  • a curvature anomaly of the refractive media
  • parallel incident light rays do not converge at a point but are drawn apart to form a line.

C) Astigmatism #36

  • Regular
  • irregular

C) Astigmatism #37

  • Regular astigmatism
  • differences between refraction of different meridians
  • not only one focus upon the retina
  • as in hypermetropia and myopia
  • two foci corresponding to the two meridians always perpendicular one to another.
  • physiological and pathological

Regular astigmatism #38

  • The two main meridians (I and II) are perpendicular to each other.
  • A punctiform object (o) is represented as a line segment Y'II and Y'I at the focal points of the two meridians.
  • Midway between these two focal points is the “circle of least confusion” (Kr), the location with the least loss of image definition.

C) Astigmatism #39

  • Regular astigmatism
  • physiological
  • pathological

Physiological astigmatism #40

  • the vertical meridian (ocular dioptric system) more refractive than the horizontal
  • flattening of eye by pressure of the superior eyelid
  • becomes a little myopic (<1D)
  • normal sight
  • needs no correction.

Pathological astigmatism #41

  • difference between the refractions of the 2 main meridians >1D
  • Any kinds of refractive differences, (no matter how small), in the favor of the horizontal.
  • Particularities.
  • present from the birth
  • stationary throughout the life;
  • transmission is hereditary dominant ;
  • lowers distance and near vision

Pathological astigmatism #42

  • Classification.
  • a) Localization of the two posterior foci.
  • simple astigmatism
  • one upon the retina and the other one behind or before it;
  • compound astigmatism
  • the both foci located either before or behind the retina
  • mixed form
  • one focus is behind the retina and the other one before it.

Pathological astigmatism #43

  • b) the vertical meridian in normal eyes is always more refractive than the horizontal one.
  • with the rule
  • against the rule
  • c) inclination of the two axes of the main refractive meridians.
  • with or without inclined axes.

Pathological astigmatism #44

  • Management.
  • Optical correction must be totally or very close to the real value of astigmatism.
  • simple astigmatism
  • cylindrical glasses ,
  • have a mark indicating the direction of the optical inactive axis;
  • the axis must be placed perpendicular on the ammetropic meridian.

Pathological astigmatism #45

  • Optical
  • a Cylinder lenses refract light only in the plane perpendicular to the axis of the cylinder.
  • The axis of the cylinder defines the nonrefracting plane.
  • b–d Cylinder lenses
  • plus cylinders (c)
  • minus cylinders (d).

Pathological astigmatism #46

  • Management.
  • Optical
  • Compound astigmatism
  • spherical and cylindrical glasses.
  • The purpose of the correction is to bring the “focal lines” of two main meridians together at one focal point.
  • requires a lens that refracts in only one plane
  • Once the two “focal lines” have been converged into a focal point, additional spherical lenses can be used to shift this focal point on to the retina

Pathological astigmatism #47

  • Management.
  • Optical
  • torric contact lenses.
  • Surgical
  • corneal refractive surgery (arcuate incisions, Excimer laser)

Irregular astigmatism #48

  • irregularities at the same median of the ocular dioptric system that result in areas with different refractions
  • Corneal ulcerations with resulting scarring of the cornea.
  • Penetrating corneal trauma.
  • Advanced keratoconus
  • Curvature and refractive power of the refractive media are totally irregular,
  • multiple focal points.

Irregular astigmatism #49

  • optical
  • hard contact lenses
  • surgical
  • corneal grafting

2.Dynamical refraction #50

  • Accommodation
  • the eye ability to alter its refraction in accordance with the distance of the object.
  • the eye is able to clearly see
  • at the infinite ( no accommodation)
  • at the different distances between infinite and eye.
  • with the help of the lens and ciliary body

Mechanism of the accommodation #51

  • Positive accommodation.
  • clearly seeing an object that comes near to the eye.
  • the ciliary muscle(ring shape fibers) contracts, the zonule relaxes and the lens bulges along its axis taking a spherical form
  • lens refractive power increases

Mechanism of the accommodation #52

  • Negative accommodation.
  • to clearly see an object that moves away from the eye
  • the ciliary muscle relaxes, stretching the zonular ligament and flattening the lens,
  • lens refractive power lowers.

2.Dynamical refraction #53

  • Accommodation
  • The ciliary muscle is innervated by the short ciliary nerves, postganglionic parasympathetic fibers of the oculomotor .
  • Parasympatholytics (atropine, cyclopentolate )inhibit the function of the ciliary muscle and prevent accommodation.

Particularities #54

  • a) Remotum point (far point)
  • the greatest distance where an eye may see without using accommodation
  • emmetropic eye this distance means the infinite;
  • myopic eye this distance is located between infinite and the eye, the greater the degree of myopia is the nearer to the eye this point is localized
  • hypermetropic eye, this point is “beyond” the infinite behind the eye.

Particularities #55

  • b) Proximum point (near point),
  • the nearest point at which the eye is able to clearly see the objects using maximum accommodation available.
  • depends upon
  • the refraction defect
  • for the myopic eye it is closer to the eye, so the greater the degree of the myopia is the closer to the eye near point is located
  • for the hypermetropic eye the proximum point is located farther off the eye so the greater the degree of hypermetropic is the farther from the eye this point is located.
  • the patient age

Particularities #56

  • c) Accommodative amplitude
  • changing the lens refraction estimated in diopters between remotum and proximum points.
  • d) Accommodative way
  • the distance in cm between remotum and proximum points.

Mechanism of the accommodation #57

  • Disturbances
  • physiological
  • nonphysiological

Physiological changes (Presbyopia) #58

  • Physiopathology and management
  • accommodative amplitude is age-related
  • steady decline with age
  • due to progressive sclerosis of the lens
  • for reading a text at 25 cm an emmetropic eye needs an accommodative amplitude of 4 D

Physiological changes (Presbyopia) #59

  • Physiopathology and management
  • at the age of 45, an emmetropic person has only 3D of accommodative amplitude
  • the characters of the print text become unclear,
  • the eye gets tired
  • tendency to move the text away from the eye
  • manifests first at the artificial light

Physiological changes (Presbyopia) #60

  • Physiopathology and management
  • correction with convergent glasses for near vision in order to supply the ocular refraction with the accommodation deficiency
  • myopic patients
  • manifests later or not at all (>3 D)
  • hypermetropic patients,
  • appears earlier
  • the greater the hypermetropia the earlier the age of appearance of presbyopia.

Nonphysiological changes #61

  • accommodative asthenopia,
  • palsy of the accommodation,
  • spasm of the accommodation.

Accommodative asthenopia #62

  • in patients with hypermetropia or small degree of astigmatism
  • tiredness of the ciliary muscle
  • overstressing the accommodation for the near vision
  • symptoms
  • frontal and periorbital pains, headaches, nausea,
  • vomiting, pain in the eye, watering, congestion
  • correction
  • glasses adequately to refractive errors

Paralysis of the accommodation #63

  • during the paralysis of the 3d cranial nerves
  • causes
  • poisonings with atropine, beladona;
  • local use of cycloplegic drugs (atropine);
  • food poisonings (botulism, diphtheria)
  • symptoms and signs
  • decreasing the near vision with normal distance vision
  • management
  • parasympathomimetic drugs (pilocarpine) locally.
  • Should become permanent, convergent glasses for near vision

Spasm of the accommodation #64

  • local use of parasympathomimetic drugs (pilocarpine)
  • general poisonings with sulphonamides
  • symptoms and signs
  • abrupt lowering the distance vision
  • maintenance of the normal near vision
  • management
  • discontinuing the use of topical substances.
